title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally, with social media and celebrities reducing taboos and influencing beauty ideals
paragraphs: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

Without question, social media has had a significant impact on the global perception of plastic surgery. Surgeons and patients commonly share detailed stories about cosmetic surgery experiences, and celebrities around the world are increasingly candid about their own procedures. This openness has reduced the taboo surrounding this once hidden area of self-investment.

One of us is a medical student, and the other is a practicing plastic surgeon who previously served as president of the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Through our research, we have identified a few key themes shaping cosmetic surgery globally.

Notably, social media has created some shared aesthetic trends, such as “Instagram Face.” Popularized by filters, this look is defined by full lips and high cheekbones, blending features from different ethnicities into one aesthetic.
But cultural identity continues to influence regional beauty standards, reflected in the different types of procedures prioritized around the world.
South Korea, often called the plastic surgery capital of the world, performs more cosmetic surgeries per capita than any other country, at roughly 16 procedures per 1,000 people.
It is also a major destination for medical tourism. About 1 in 10 cosmetic surgery patients in South Korea travel from abroad, primarily from China, Japan and the U.S.
In this market, K-pop and K-drama celebrities are widely seen as setting the standard for beauty.

More than 70% of cosmetic surgeries in South Korea are facial procedures. The most popular and well-known procedure is double eyelid surgery, which creates a crease in the upper eyelid, a feature that about half of East Asians are born without. Other common procedures include facial fat grafting, brow lifts and rhinoplasties.

Cosmetic surgery is widely accepted in South Korean culture, and it is viewed as an investment for social and professional success, rather than an act of vanity. One survey found that 90% of South Korean women ages 20 to 69 had been exposed to cosmetic surgery advertising.

China’s cosmetic surgery market is one of the fastest growing in the world, with 1.4 million cosmetic surgeries performed in 2025 – a rate of 1 surgery per 1,000 people. As in South Korea, procedures were predominantly focused on the face, and the No. 1 procedure was eyelid surgery.

A survey of Chinese female college students found that the top influences in getting cosmetic surgery were peers, pressure to stand out in an extremely competitive job market and social media exposure.

Social media has helped codify and perpetuate specific beauty ideals. For example, the term “melon seed face” was coined to describe the traditional Chinese beauty standard of an oval face shape with a slim, V-shaped jawline.

China’s plastic surgery market is simultaneously redefining how consumers find and access procedures. More than 60,000 plastic surgery clinics use platforms like Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, to advertise their services.
Dedicated cosmetic surgery apps such as GengMei and SoYoung increase accessibility by using AI to analyze users’ faces, connecting them with local clinics and even helping finance surgery payments.

While Brazil is the seventh-largest country in the world by population, it ranks first in the total number of cosmetic procedures performed globally. This market performed approximately 2.4 million surgeries at a rate of 11 per 1,000 people in 2025.

In contrast to South Korea and China, which emphasize facial procedures, Brazil’s market is defined by body contouring. In fact, this is true for much of Latin America. Liposuction – a surgery that uses suction to remove body fat – is the most commonly performed procedure, followed by breast augmentations and abdominal and buttock procedures.

Brazil’s emphasis on body shape and lower body aesthetics is so well known that it inspired the name of one of the world’s most popular procedures – the Brazilian Butt Lift, or BBL – despite the fact that it may not have actually originated in Brazil.

Cosmetic surgery in Brazil is highly accessible across all socioeconomic classes, rooted in the philosophy that everyone has a “right to beauty.” Brazil is one of the only countries where public hospitals offer cosmetic surgery for free to those who cannot afford it.

The U.S. ranked second globally in cosmetic surgery volume, just behind Brazil, with approximately 2.2 million procedures in 2025, at a rate of about 6.5 surgeries per 1,000 people. And like Brazil, the U.S. predominantly performs body contouring surgeries over facial surgeries.

The U.S. is unique in that it performs the highest number of nonsurgical procedures, such as fillers, botox and chemical peels. This may reflect a growing preference for subtle changes through minor, short-term treatments over major surgical makeovers.

Turkey is one of the world’s top destinations for medical tourism. According to Turkey’s Ministry of Health, more than 1.5 million people traveled to Turkey for medical procedures in 2024, generating US$3 billion in revenue.

This is largely driven by Turkey’s hair transplant industry, with numerous high-volume clinics offering low-cost procedures and travel packages. The Turkish Health Tourism Association estimated 1 million tourists spent $2 billion for hair transplants in 2022 alone.

Besides hair transplants, Turkey performs approximately 800,000 cosmetic surgeries annually, at a rate of nine surgeries per 1,000 people. Roughly 30% of patients travel from abroad for these procedures, primarily from Germany, the U.K. and the U.S.

title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
paragraphs: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year.
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026.
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.

Suvrat Dhanorkar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
paragraphs: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young has received donations from NVIDIA academic hardware grant programs in the past and has coauthored academic publications with current and former NVIDIA employees.

title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
paragraphs: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox, an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17, which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.
The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23, compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.
In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.
The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials.
Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.
Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980. But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II. The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos, a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two, compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses.
In the U.S., a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women estimated 89% protection with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose.

In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but only 35% among people living with HIV – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection.

There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels drop sharply between six and 12 months after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection.

title: How the construction, desecration and destruction of Jerusalem’s ancient temples shaped Judaism – and Hanukkah
paragraphs: In 167 B.C.E., on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. According to tradition, he converted the sanctuary to a temple to Zeus. More broadly, Antiochos outlawed Jewish customs, including dietary laws, circumcision and observing the Sabbath.
The name Epiphanes meant “manifest,” implying the king was a god on Earth, but Jewish sources called him “Epimanes”: madman.

Three years later, on the same day of the same month, Jews in Jerusalem scored a major victory against the Greeks, and the Temple was converted back to a Jewish place of worship. Rabbinic texts written much later described how one day’s worth of oil, all that was left to rededicate the Temple, lasted for eight – the seeming miracle at the heart of the Hanukkah story.

The holiday’s name means “dedication,” highlighting the temple’s importance for Jewish cultures. This temple, in fact, was the second version, after the first place of worship to the Jewish deity was destroyed in 586 B.C.E..
As a scholar of the Bible and religions drawn from it, I am fascinated by the history of the two temples in Jerusalem, which are vital for understanding the background of Hanukkah.

In ancient West Asia, temples played a pivotal role in religion, politics, the economy and even family life. In many ways, for example, they functioned like modern banks, where taxes would be collected and storehouses of treasuries accumulated.

Temples also served as the house of the god or goddess worshipped there. At a temple at Ain Dara, in modern-day Syria, carvings of 10-foot-long (3-meter-long) footsteps represent a deity entering its abode. Several times, the Bible refers to the temple in Jerusalem as the “house of the LORD.”

The first major temple in Jerusalem is traditionally thought to have been built by King Solomon in the 10th century B.C.E. Nothing of Solomon’s temple remains, but the Bible’s Book of 1 Kings describes three main sections: an outer portico, a main hall and the “holy of holies,” an inner sanctuary.

The ancient Israelites’ belief that God resided in that sanctuary was foundational to the often-bewildering sets of rituals performed at the Temple. These laws, laid out in the biblical Book of Leviticus, were designed to keep the divine abode ritually pure.

After all, if the most powerful being ever lived in the Temple, keeping it clean, and keeping God happy there, would be of paramount importance. When the divine presence settled in the Temple, biblical authors claimed, Jerusalem could not be destroyed.

After Solomon’s reign, ancient Israel split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south, where Jerusalem lay. Assyrians, whose large empire lay to the east, conquered the north in the eighth century B.C.E., and before long, their armies tried to invade Jerusalem, too. They failed, fueling biblical writers’ conviction that Jerusalem was inviolable so long as God lived there.

But over the years, the Bible describes religious observance in Judah growing lax. As the Book of Ezekiel tells it, God departed his dwelling, leaving it open to destruction by the Babylonians in 586 B.C.E.

In the ancient world, many cultures believed that when a temple was destroyed, the god who dwelt there lost a battle. The victors tended to cart away images of the conquered cultures’ deities, an act called “god-napping.” Some of those divinities would be absorbed into the conquering culture’s traditions.

After Judah’s defeat, its people were exiled to Babylon, where Iraq and Syria are today. Yet the exiled Judeans’ traditions did not disappear. Instead, they found ways to innovate. In place of the Temple and the sacrifices made there, they built houses of worship called “synagogues” and developed new services and prayers.
About 50 years later, however, the Judeans received a second chance to create a divine dwelling in Jerusalem. Cyrus, king of Persia, decreed that they could return and build a second temple.

When this new structure was erected around 520 B.C.E., it proved initially disappointing. According to the Bible’s Book of Ezra, those who had seen the First Temple wept for sorrow since the second was a pale reflection of the first.

Not that this was the only temple: There is archaeological evidence of one in Egypt in the fifth century B.C.E.; and another, even earlier, in Tel Motza, just a few miles from Solomon’s Temple. Scholars debate how temples were perceived in ancient Judah, since the Bible’s Book of Deuteronomy suggests that only the one temple in Jerusalem should exist.
Despite the evidence for these other temples, surviving Jewish tradition has only emphasized these two – the First and Second – in Jerusalem.

It was the Second Temple that became the object of Antiochus’ persecution – a persecution that, according to some scholars, was the first religiously motivated one in history. Prior empires in the region cared little for local religious observances, as long as subjects paid taxes to the central authorities.

One motivation behind Antiochus’ actions may have been economic: His empire was losing ground, and fast, in an expensive struggle against the Romans, whose power in the Mediterranean was quickly growing. Jewish communities paid a tax to the Temple in Jerusalem, so robbing its treasures may have been an attempt to replenish the empire’s depleted finances.

Ultimately the Jewish community in Jerusalem won out against Antiochus’ persecution. Over a century later, under King Herod, the Second Temple was expanded to become quite a marvel. Even Roman sources described it as a splendid edifice. His reconstruction project would continue long after his life, into the early 60s C.E.
Only a few years later, in 70, the Romans destroyed the Second Temple. The Western Wall of the compound survives today as a testimony to Herod’s expansive construction project.
Today, the place where the First and Second Temples once stood is called the Temple Mount. There has not been a third temple, despite some groups’ calls to build one.

Though Jews no longer perform temple rites, studying those laws is a major focus of the Talmud, a collection of rabbinic rulings and debates. And as Hanukkah demonstrates, Jewish communities celebrate the temples through liturgy, literature and ritual. As Jews around the world light their menorahs, the holiday is a reminder of the Temple’s importance, even if it no longer exists.

title: Why American consumers are still spending and powering the US economy – and why this could soon fizzle
paragraphs: Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers. With inflation fatigue, declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back?

This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering.

Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than what was expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates, consumer spending held up remarkably well.

I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way.
What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many people to keep up.
Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous.

Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands, shopping at off-brand and discount stores, or relentlessly hunting for deals. Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans.

“Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect, and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce.
These are both responses to the rising cost of living.
More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make some extra cash.

About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter – whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn extra discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn.

Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges.

According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the actual number of donors is dropping.
Many consumers are now running out of levers to pull.
Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip, which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest.

One in four families are spending more than they make, as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago.

For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high. Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences. Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise.

And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now – with unemployment at 4.1% – is critical. If this healthy job market holds and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise, Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink – and hurt economic growth in the process.
That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady.

Whether it comes to this, it’s important to remember that the holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down?

Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers are facing challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 – but that’s far from a sure thing.
Chris Gaffney has received funding from the U.S. Department of Commerce's Economic Development Administration.

title: Why expect holiday traditions to stay the same, even as life continually changes?
paragraphs: There’s something about the holiday season that makes people notice the passage of time. As you unpack treasured decorations, prepare family recipes and listen to familiar holiday songs, you’re reminded not only of celebrations from years past but also of different times in your life.

With each passing year, children grow older, families welcome new members, relationships change, and some of those you once celebrated with are no longer here. But people often approach the holidays hoping to experience them just as they once did.

As someone who studies life transitions, I’m particularly interested in why people expect traditional holiday celebrations to remain the same when so much else in life has changed. I suggest thinking of holiday memories not as a blueprint for recreating the past but as a way to understand what makes these times meaningful to you, and how you might carry that meaning into the present.

Research on family rituals suggests that traditions contribute to a sense of identity and belonging by connecting you to the people, experiences and shared values that have shaped your life. In fact, research focused on holiday rituals has found that participating in traditions such as preparing grandmother’s chocolate fudge or watching favorite seasonal movies is associated with greater feelings of closeness and enjoyment during celebrations.

You may not recognize how tightly some holiday traditions are tied to certain stages of your life. Parents who once looked forward to Christmas morning with young children may now find themselves coordinating celebrations around the schedules of adult children and their families and in-laws. Someone who has hosted holiday gatherings for decades may find themselves adjusting to being a guest rather than orchestrating the festivities.
Although these kinds of changes are a natural part of life, they can bring a mix of emotions. You can welcome new experiences while still missing aspects of an earlier time.
During these periods of transition, the memories associated with holiday traditions may become especially meaningful, offering a connection to the past as you adjust to the present.

If you find yourself missing the holidays of years past, you may be longing not for the celebration itself but for a particular era. Memories of former times can bring comfort, but they can also evoke feelings of grief, loneliness or sadness, particularly if you’re navigating changes you didn’t anticipate or would not have chosen, such as illness, injury, unemployment or relationship breakdown.
People may be more inclined to experience nostalgia, a sentimental longing for the past, during periods of transition, when familiar aspects of life are changing.
While nostalgia is sometimes viewed negatively, as dwelling on past experiences, research suggests it can be a valuable resource when navigating life changes, especially for younger generations.

For instance, nostalgia can actually strengthen social connections and contribute to a sense of meaning. Recalling cherished memories can remind you you’re part of a broader life story, which can enhance feelings of connection, personal value and purpose.
Nostalgia can also help people make sense of the different chapters of life, allowing them to maintain a sense of who they are even as circumstances change.

Memories, then, can be more than reminders of what once was. They can help you recognize what you value and inform how you experience the present. While nostalgia may not ease the pain associated with challenges such as major health changes, evolving caregiving responsibilities or military deployment, it can serve as a bridge between the past and the present.

Throughout life, people adjust routines, responsibilities and expectations to accommodate new circumstances. Yet when it comes to the holidays, they may be reluctant to make those same adjustments. Is it still Thanksgiving if the table doesn’t feature the cranberry sauce made with your family’s traditional recipe? Can it feel like Christmas if there’s no tree decorated with your family’s sentimental ornaments?

This reluctance to let holiday observances evolve may be influenced, in part, by how people remember previous celebrations. Negative emotions associated with past experiences tend to fade more quickly than positive ones. You may remember the warmth of gathering around a holiday table but less readily recall the stress or challenges that accompanied it.

When expectations no longer reflect the realities of your life, you may feel disappointed or place pressure on yourself or others to live up to those old memories. Even a cherished tradition can become a source of stress when you feel obligated to maintain it in the same way year after year.

As you navigate life’s transitions, it may be helpful to reflect on what you cherish most about your holiday traditions. Is it the way you have always celebrated? Or is it the feelings of comfort and belonging that you associate with those celebrations?
Research suggests that reflecting on the past can inspire people to seek meaningful connections and experiences in the present.

Of course, adjusting to change is not always easy, and for some, the holidays can be particularly hard. Adapting does not mean abandoning cherished traditions, directly replacing what has been lost, or feeling pressured to create new memories. It may simply mean accepting that the holidays will feel different and allowing yourself the time and space to adjust.

In the desire to recreate what once was, many people may overlook the moments that could become cherished memories in the years ahead. Savor the memories of holidays past without expecting them to define how you experience the holidays today. Celebrations don’t need to remain the same to remain meaningful.

Lee Ann Rawlins Williams does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Immersive shopping has survived the demise of the metaverse – but its appeal depends on how it’s designed and who is using it
paragraphs: In 2021 and 2022, major retailers and fashion brands were racing into the metaverse, opening virtual stores, creating digital products and inviting consumers to explore branded worlds through avatars. Much of that excitement has since faded. But the technologies behind those experiments are far from disappearing.

Today, shoppers can try on clothes virtually, see how furniture would look in their homes and explore branded worlds on gaming platforms. Rather than building entirely new virtual universes, retailers are finding ways to integrate immersive technologies into familiar shopping experiences.

A 2025 global survey found that 53% of surveyed retail professionals focused on virtual fitting rooms, while 46% said they were building augmented reality and virtual reality experiences. On the consumer side, a 2024 survey of more than 2,200 U.S. shoppers found that 49% of respondents would buy more clothing if a great virtual try-on experience were available. Meanwhile, a separate survey found that only 4.5% of U.S. digital shoppers regularly used these technologies for shopping.
Immersive technologies continue to attract interest, but their regular use in online shopping remains limited. So what makes an immersive shopping experience worth using?

I’m a scholar of retail and consumer sciences who studies consumers’ interactions with technology in the retail environment. My research suggests that the value of immersive retail isn’t simply about how advanced or realistic the technology is. It’s about how the experience is designed, how it addresses consumers’ needs and how it helps them connect with products and brands.

Imagine shopping for a pair of sunglasses online. You like the style, but you’re not sure how they would look on you. Amazon allows shoppers to try on certain shoes and eyewear virtually using their smartphones. IKEA applies a similar concept to home furnishings through IKEA Kreativ, which allows customers to digitally remove existing furniture from their rooms and experiment with new arrangements.
These experiences address a fundamental limitation of online shopping: the gap between seeing a product on a screen and imagining how it would look on you or in your own space.

My colleagues and I found that the experience of virtually trying on clothes can be particularly helpful for shoppers who struggle to imagine how clothing would look on them. By making it easier to visualize themselves wearing a product, the technology can help them feel more comfortable with their purchase decisions. In other words, the value of immersive technology may lie less in creating a sense of novelty than in helping consumers overcome the limitations of conventional online shopping.

As artificial intelligence advances, so-called virtual try-on experiences are becoming increasingly personalized. Shoppers can now see clothing on digital representations of themselves rather than relying solely on images of fashion models. It might seem intuitive that the more closely a virtual model resembles a shopper, the better the experience. But our research suggests otherwise.

In two experiments, we found that consumers’ responses to personalized avatars depend on what psychologists call “assessment orientation,” or the tendency to critically evaluate and compare options before making a decision. This mindset of carefully thinking through a decision can also shift depending on the shopping situation, such as choosing an outfit for a job interview versus casually browsing for fun.

Shoppers with a stronger evaluative mindset, whether due to their personal tendencies or the shopping situation, felt a stronger sense that they were the model and expressed greater intentions to buy when using personalized 3D avatars than when viewing conventional model images. Interestingly, the opposite pattern emerged among shoppers who are less inclined to mull over options.

The implication is that the same technology can offer different value to different consumers. A highly personalized experience may be particularly useful to someone who wants to thoroughly evaluate a product, but it isn’t necessarily better for everyone or every shopping situation.
Immersive technologies can also offer value beyond helping consumers decide what to buy.

Walmart, for example, has created branded experiences on Roblox, where users can explore virtual spaces, play games and discover digital products. These experiences offer retailers a new way to connect with younger consumers and build brand engagement through entertainment rather than traditional advertising. Its Walmart Discovered Roblox gaming environment has attracted nearly 40 million visits as of May 2026.

My research on branded virtual worlds suggests that simply creating a virtual space isn’t enough to engage consumers. What matters is how brands bring these spaces to life through storytelling and social experiences that help consumers feel more connected to the brand. The value of these environments lies less in their 3D graphics than in the opportunities they create for consumers to participate, interact and become part of a brand’s story.

Advances in AI will likely open up even more possibilities for immersive online shopping, from more realistic virtual try-on to interactive environments that adapt to individual preferences. But making an experience more technologically sophisticated doesn’t automatically make it more valuable.

Whether a retailer’s goal is to help shoppers visualize products, make more informed decisions or build connections with brands, they are more likely to be successful if they design experiences around consumers rather than around the capabilities of the technology.

title: Columbia is keeping its gates closed, raising the question of what universities owe their neighborhoods
paragraphs: The Gaza war protests that overtook some colleges and universities in 2023 and 2024 have long dispersed – but one very clear remnant of the demonstrations remains at Columbia University’s Morningside Heights campus in New York City: a closed campus.

Columbia’s administration first shut the gates in April 2024, following pro-Palestinian rights protests and waves of police arrests. New York City politicians said that these disruptions were fueled by “outside agitators.”
Now, only students, faculty, staff and alumni with a school ID are able to enter Columbia’s quad.

Some of Columbia’s neighbors sued the university in January 2025, saying that the closure created a “six-block barrier between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue from West 120th to West 114th Street” and violated the Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act.

A New York Supreme Court judge in Manhattan dismissed their suit on Nov. 10, 2026, saying that “even if Columbia previously granted unrestricted public access to College Walk, as it remained their private property, nothing prevented them from restricting access at any time.” The plaintiffs quickly appealed the decision.
Columbia has maintained that safety concerns meant it needed to close its gates, and that the campus is private property.

Nonetheless, in the past, Columbia allowed neighbors to cross the campus as a scenic shortcut through the neighborhood. Nearby nursery schools used the campus green as a place for children to explore and play.

As a college professor of law and political science, and an elected official in the western Massachusetts town where I teach, the Columbia campus controversy feels familiar. These “town-and-gown” disputes have, from time to time, raised questions about what universities owe the community beyond their gates.

From at least the 1950s until 2024, Columbia had an open campus policy. In 1953, New York City approved closing the campus’s central West 116th Street stretch to cars, with the understanding that pedestrians would be able to walk across the campus.

The recent closure stirred up tensions between the school and its neighbors. But such strains are as old as universities themselves. Some commentators suggest that conflict between universities and their surrounding communities can be traced back to medieval Europe.

“The early universities in cities such as Bologna and Paris took a very different form to the institutions we know today. They were loose communities of masters and scholars who lived amongst the people of the town,” the education historian Harley Richardson wrote in 2020.

Townspeople often resented those scholars and students because “They couldn’t understand the scholarly Latin spoken by the students” or whether “the long gowns they wore” were “intended to convey a superior social status,” Richardson wrote.

One of the most notorious town-gown incidents that turned violent occurred in Oxford, England, in February 1354 on so-called St. Scholastica Day, honoring an Italian saint who founded the order of the Benedictine nuns.

Trouble began in a local tavern when some students complained loudly and aggressively about the poor quality of the wine they were served. Things escalated when the tavern-keeper, who was also the mayor of Oxford, responded with insults. A fight broke out and drew in a large number of townspeople and students who rushed to the scene. It took the intervention of the king to restore order.
Conflicts between universities and their local towns or cities have also been very much a part of the story of higher education in the United States.
Most often these disputes have focused on issues like where a university should build a dormitory or whether it should pay fees to the city where it is located.
And as in England, these conflicts have occasionally turned violent.
One such incident happened in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1806, when riots broke out between Yale University students and locals who were on their way to church.
What, if anything, do universities owe their communities?

The popular phrase “the ivory tower” captures one vision of a university. It suggests that universities serve society by being left alone to conduct research and educate students, disengaged from the larger community’s immediate concerns. In this view, people outside of universities benefit indirectly from the inventions and innovations that universities produce, as well as from the jobs they create.

Another vision, which came to prominence in the 1960s, called on universities to be good citizens of their surrounding communities. This view urged university leaders to invest in their neighborhoods.

Colby College, in Waterville, Maine, exemplifies this approach. It has spent US$265 million on construction and other investment projects over the past several years, with an eye on revitalizing its struggling downtown district.

Others schools, including the University of Notre Dame, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Southern California and the University of California, San Francisco, have invested substantial amounts of money in developing their towns and cities and supporting neighbors. Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut, for example, announced in September 2026 that it would pay for the full tuition, housing and meals for local residents who are admitted as students.

Some universities have been sending students out into the communities around them as one way to support their city. For example, Columbia Journalism School students are often tasked with developing a reporting project in a particular New York City neighborhood.

title: Georgians mark 2 years of pro-EU demonstrations – defying campaign to wear protesters down
paragraphs: For months on end, Georgians have braved the elements and long odds to protest their government’s suspension of the former Soviet country’s bid to join the European Union. On Nov. 28, 2026, those pro-democracy campaigners will mark a milestone – two years of sustained, if declining, protest.

Hailed as a beacon of democracy following its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Georgia has of late been increasingly held up as an example of democratic backsliding: the slow, persistent erosion of democratic institutions. Indeed, the 2025 Economist Democracy Index — an annual benchmark of global democratic health — found that Georgia had fallen 20 places on the list since 2017.

The formal hallmarks of democratic systems remain visible: Elections are held, parliaments vote and political parties organize. At the same time, democratic institutions are compromised by political leaders, parties, police, courts and legislators – who use their resources to stifle dissent and compromise democratic institutions .

These leaders commonly target electoral fairness without committing blatant fraud. For example, public sector workers such as teachers are threatened with job loss if they do not vote for the government, or local governments are rewarded for producing votes during elections. Critics allege that biased laws and politicized court cases eliminate independent media and jail opposition leaders.

Backsliding governments also use disinformation and rhetoric to create confusion and fear. Using these tactics, critics allege, the ruling populist right, pro-Russian Georgian Dream government continues to undermine the fragile democracy. With many feeling unable to fight back through elections and parliamentary debates, Georgians have taken to the streets.

I am a member of a research project that explores how national protests in countries with fragile democratic institutions create legacies that can influence politics over the long term. In Georgia, that work is based on interviews with leaders from across civic and political life. These interviews point to a widespread view that the government is actively attempting to erode protest just as critics of the government feel it has eroded institutions. So far, the government has not crushed the movement with a campaign of lethal force. Rather, it has tried to use lower-level, but sustained, suppression tactics in hopes of inducing burnout in the opposition and getting civil society to disengage.

In Georgia, the roots of protest are deep in the struggle for independence from the Soviet Union and the influence of Russia under the leadership of Vladimir Putin. In 2003, Georgians launched the Rose Revolution – the first in a series of actions across the former Soviet states called the Color Revolutions – to support democracy and autonomy from the Russian Federation.

The Georgian Dream emerged as a socially conservative opposition party in 2012 under the leadership of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili and won a majority of seats in parliamentary elections. Many analysts at the time saw the party as a new chance to consolidate democracy. Yet unable to provide economic gains, the party instead embarked on a platform consistent with pro-Russian security policies, which critics allege were rife with political manipulation, and false rhetoric that undermined democracy. In 2019, Georgians took to the streets to contest failed electoral reforms and growing Russian influence through Ivanishvili’s governance.

By 2023, tens of thousands of Georgians filled Rustaveli Avenue in the capital of Tbilisi to oppose a law designed to shutter civic organizations and independent media. The so-called Russia Law borrowed heavily from the Kremlin’s tactics to eliminate opposition to the Putin government in Russia. Many Georgians understood the law as an attack on democracy and celebrated when the ruling party, Georgian Dream, withdrew its bill.

A year later, as new elections approached, the party reintroduced the law, provoking renewed protest. This time it passed. A few months later, preelection polls showed the opposition parties leading, but expectations of victory evaporated when Georgia Dream secured 54% of vote – an outcome that critics raised as a possible indicator of electoral manipulation.

Then, on Nov. 28, 2024, the new government put Georgia’s European Union bid on hold until 2028. Many Georgians have long seen EU membership as a path forward to economic growth and democratic protections. In light of Russia’s 2008 occupation of Georgian territory and 2022 full-scale war in Ukraine, Georgians also perceived EU membership as a bulwark against Russian intervention.

Fueled by feelings of betrayal over the reversal on EU membership, crowds poured back onto Rustaveli Avenue, reaching a peak of 170,000-200,000 protesters. Several hundred activists have returned every day since.

Over the course of two years, Georgian protesters have faced chronic and unpredictable violence rather than a decisive crackdown. By Amnesty International’s count, thousands have been arrested, hundreds beaten in the streets or abused in custody, and more than 150 imprisoned after politically motivated trials.

In general, however, the Georgian government’s tactic for countering the protest movement has been to avoid mass violence in lieu of targeted attacks on protest leaders and subtler means to discourage new activists. Fines for protest rose tenfold between 2024 and 2026 to double the average Georgian’s monthly income, leading Amnesty International to conclude that Georgia’s courts have become tools for “financially exhausting protesters.” Meanwhile, repeat offenses for participating in a demonstration have become crimes.

These actions have steadily increased the costs of protesting, driving activists from the streets due to a multitude of reasons related to risk, personal safety and fear. In our research, we protect the people we interviewed from state retaliation by making them anonymous.
The effects of these costs are clear in their statements.
“We don’t say it openly,” an investigative journalist and editor told us. “But the truth is, we were exhausted, depleted — and that’s the state we were in when the election campaign started.”

Another pro-European student movement member said, “Human resources are exhausted. You can’t expect 300,000 or 100,000 or even 20,000 people to march from Ilia University to Parliament every single day for 200 or 300 days straight. People have jobs, lives, personal struggles, and you can’t ask them to drop everything every day.”

Overall, our interviews with a variety of civil society leaders and protest supporters found that exhaustion was widespread and that a declining amount of people had the physical, financial or emotional capacity to stand every day.

Still, leaders remain hopeful that the nightly protests will provide a platform for renewed activism when the next opportunity for challenging the government presents itself. As the same pro-European student movement member argued: “I believe that will change. Let’s say Georgians are just on a kind of protest vacation. I hope we’ll be back out there again, all together, very soon.”

For now, there exists an effective stalemate between the protest movement and the government. The movement endures but has not broken through, and I believe the government cannot crush it because it fears the student leader is right — and the protest vacation might end.
For a generation of Georgians invested in building democracy, the past two years have shown how quickly democratic gains can be undone.

Still, as the anniversary of nightly protests approaches, many Georgians point to Serbia, where student protesters also took the streets in November 2024 and forced an early election on Oct. 25, 2026. The same Serbian students formed an opposition bloc that won a parliamentary majority that unseated an entrenched and increasingly autocratic leader.
Georgian Dream understands this threat and has proposed a ban on opposition parties, closing the route that Serbia’s students used.

title: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it
paragraphs: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the pop art scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the source of her creativity. Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications.
Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world?

Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created Accumulation No. 1, her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical Infinity Mirror Rooms installation.
A major retrospective of her work is on view at the Stedelijk Museum through Jan. 17, 2027.

The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an art historian who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.

Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the male-dominated New York art world. During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants.

Painter Grace Hartigan had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.

Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond abstract expressionism. The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality coded as masculine. Pop artists refused this model: They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production.

Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show. She decided to focus on sewing — an art rooted in her female Japanese education — and she ordered a sewing machine.

Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a symbol of patriarchal authority – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft.
In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.

Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis. But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.

In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped sew the protrusions on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.

Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while she was exploring “kyōfu” – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for the uncanny is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called penis envy.
Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a satire of penis envy. And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power.

In one of her self-portraits from 1966, Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist Louise Bourgeois, who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including Fillette (Little Girl), that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.

But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times gave her work only a brief mention. When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he received rave reviews in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.

Kusama’s popularity today stems from works that are both visually expansive and socially subversive. Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show was her first all-over exhibit – an exhibition in which a repeated motif covers the gallery’s four walls, drawing the audience into the work rather than asking them to view it as a separate object. On display at the Gertrude Stein Gallery from December 1963 to January 1964, it featured a sculpture of the phallus-embedded boat surrounded by its image repeating across the wall.

Although Kusama sought to subvert male authority, she appears nude in a photograph of the phallus boat installation, her back to the camera, trapped between the real and the illusory. Rowing the boat seems like the only way to escape the omnipresence of masculinity.
She seemed even more entrapped by patriarchal symbolism in her Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli’s Field, where she lays among an array of phalluses covered in red polka dots.

In 1966, Kusama found a way to break away from male domination through her “Peep Show” at the Castellane Gallery in New York. In it, she reduced the towering phallus to a small dot of light. It was her first work of psychedelic art, a category the curator Christoph Grunenberg characterized as both “artistic experiment and dissenting politics.”

Incorporating Beatles music, flickering strobe lights and mirror reflections, “Peep Show” was intended to produce effects similar to those of psychoactive drugs such as mescaline, psilocybin and LSD, liberating users from established social norms and opening the possibility of alternative values. The exhibit, later known as “Love Forever,” also aimed to alter perception by inducing synesthesia — a neurological state in which stimulating one sensory-cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another.

Kusama remembered attending a lecture by Timothy Leary, a former Harvard University psychology professor and psychedelics advocate, at the Village Theater in New York, a hub of psychedelic culture. In 1968, she collaborated with light artist Joshua White on Self-Obliteration, a fusion of sound, lights and images that Leary claimed “would demonstrate what an LSD session is like.”

Kusama’s ability to transform any neurosis she may have had into liberation began with Accumulation No. 1 and continued through Fireflies on the Water (2002), Soul Under the Moon (2002), Infinity Mirror Room—Aftermath of Obliteration of Eternity (2009) and Infinity Mirrored Room—The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away (2013). The ethereal visions embodied in her psychedelic mirror rooms stand in for the mind-altering drugs that release people from the rationality of society and fuel the desire to change.

title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
paragraphs: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.
My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure. Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding, including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes. Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials.

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years. Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories.

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly. In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes.

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow.” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.
To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “I’m not going to abandon my house. It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding, but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage. I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.
If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost, and some left.

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods. But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.
Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.
